top_level_objectives: Visualize how electron domain repulsion dictates the three-dimensional arrangement of atoms around a central atom.
Identify and construct the five fundamental electron-domain geometries.
Distinguish between electron-domain geometry and molecular geometry by analyzing the effect of lone pairs.
Explain and predict bond angle deviations based on the greater spatial volume occupied by lone pairs.
Apply VSEPR rules to predict complex geometries for molecules with expanded octets.

scenes.brief_purpose: To introduce the foundational concept of VSEPR theory by showing how generic electron domains automatically arrange themselves to minimize electrostatic repulsion.
key_visuals: A central atomic sphere floating in the AR workspace.
Glowing, balloon-like lobes representing generic electron domains.
Dynamic physics simulations showing domains pushing away from one another when added.
student_actions: Add generic electron domains to the central atom one at a time (from 2 up to 4 domains).
Observe the domains physically repel each other and snap into stable linear, trigonal planar, and tetrahedral arrangements.
Freely rotate the resulting structures to verify symmetry.

scenes.brief_purpose: To formalize the five basic electron-domain geometries using real molecules with only bonding pairs.
key_visuals: Interactive 3D models of BeCl2, BF3, CH4, PF5, and SF6.
Holographic protractor tools that overlay onto the models.
A virtual data table summarizing domain counts and ideal bond angles.
student_actions: Select and place each of the five fundamental molecule models into the primary workspace.
Use the holographic protractor to measure and record the idealized bond angles for each geometry (180, 120, 109.5, 90/120, 90 degrees).
Match each physical model to its correct geometric name (e.g., trigonal bipyramidal, octahedral) in the virtual table.

scenes.scene_name: Lone Pairs: Molecular vs. Electron-Domain Geometry
scenes.brief_purpose: To demonstrate how replacing bonding pairs with lone pairs changes the observable molecular shape, using the tetrahedral family as a primary example.
key_visuals: Side-by-side 3D models of Methane (CH4), Ammonia (NH3), and Water (H2O).
Toggleable visual representations of lone pair electron clouds (ghostly translucent lobes).
Floating Lewis structures corresponding to each 3D molecule.
student_actions: Toggle the visibility of lone pairs on Ammonia and Water to see how the underlying tetrahedral electron-domain geometry remains constant.
Turn off the lone pair visibility to isolate the molecular geometry (the positions of the nuclei).
Label the resulting molecular geometries (tetrahedral, trigonal pyramidal, bent).

scenes.brief_purpose: To explain why real-world bond angles deviate from idealized VSEPR angles by examining the spatial volume of lone pairs.
key_visuals: Magnified, overlaid models of CH4 (109.5 deg), NH3 (107.3 deg), and H2O (104.5 deg).
Animated electron density maps showing lone pairs occupying a wider angular volume than bonding pairs.
Live dynamic angle readouts that update as electron cloud parameters change.
student_actions: Use a slider to increase the spatial volume of the lone pair(s) on NH3 and H2O to simulate their actual electron density.
Observe the bonding pairs being physically squeezed together as the lone pair volume expands.
Correlate the expanded lone pair volume with the decreasing bond angles shown on the live readouts.

scenes.brief_purpose: To apply VSEPR theory to molecules with 5 or 6 electron domains containing lone pairs, predicting where lone pairs will reside to minimize 90-degree repulsions.
key_visuals: A trigonal bipyramidal base model (like PF5) and an octahedral base model (like SF6).
Interactive placeholders on the axial and equatorial positions of the central atoms.
A 'Repulsion Score' meter that calculates the energy of the current configuration based on 90-degree lone pair interactions.
student_actions: Attempt to place a lone pair in the axial versus equatorial position of a trigonal bipyramidal shape.
Observe the 'Repulsion Score' to discover that equatorial placement is lower energy, creating a seesaw shape (e.g., SF4).
Construct complex geometries like T-shaped (ClF3), square planar (XeF4), and square pyramidal by strategically placing lone pairs in the lowest-energy configurations.
